items.label: Water temperature
items.text: For most brewing methods, water just off the boil, around 90 to 96 degrees Celsius, extracts coffee well. Much cooler water tastes sour and thin; boiling water can taste harsh.

items.label: Grind size
items.text: Grind size controls how fast water extracts flavor. Espresso needs a fine grind, pour-over a medium grind, and French press a coarse grind so the brew is not muddy or bitter.

items.label: Brew ratio
items.text: A common starting ratio is about 1 gram of coffee to 15 to 17 grams of water. Use more coffee for a stronger cup rather than steeping for longer.

items.label: Espresso
items.text: Espresso forces hot water through a compact bed of finely ground coffee at about 9 bar of pressure. A shot usually takes 25 to 30 seconds and has a layer of crema on top.

items.label: French press
items.text: In a French press the grounds steep in the water for about four minutes before a metal mesh filter is pressed down. The metal filter lets oils through, giving a fuller body.

items.label: Pour-over
items.text: Pour-over brewing means pouring water slowly over grounds in a paper filter. Many people pour a little first to let the coffee bloom and release gas for about 30 seconds.

items.label: Cold brew
items.text: Cold brew steeps coarse grounds in cold water for 12 to 24 hours. It tastes smoother and less acidic, and is often made as a concentrate to dilute later.

items.label: Roast levels
items.text: Light roasts keep more of the bean's fruity and floral flavors. Dark roasts taste more of chocolate and smoke, as longer roasting breaks down acids and creates bitter compounds.

items.label: Storing beans
items.text: Coffee beans stay fresh longest whole, in an airtight container away from light, heat and moisture. Ground coffee goes stale within days because more surface is exposed to air.

items.label: Arabica and robusta
items.text: Arabica beans are grown at higher altitudes and taste sweeter and more complex. Robusta plants are hardier and their beans have roughly twice the caffeine and a more bitter taste.

items.label: Waggle dance
items.text: A forager bee that finds good flowers returns to the hive and performs a waggle dance. The angle of the dance shows the direction relative to the sun, and its length shows the distance.

items.label: Colony roles
items.text: A honeybee colony has one queen, thousands of female worker bees and, in warmer months, some male drones. Drones do not gather food; their role is to mate with queens from other colonies.

items.label: The queen
items.text: The queen is the only bee in the colony that lays eggs, and in summer she can lay over a thousand a day. Workers raise a new queen by feeding a young larva a diet of royal jelly.

items.label: Making honey
items.text: Bees collect nectar, mix it with enzymes and store it in wax cells. They fan their wings to evaporate water until the nectar thickens into honey, then cap the cells with wax.

items.label: Worker life
items.text: A summer worker bee lives about five to six weeks. She starts by cleaning cells and feeding larvae inside the hive, and only in her last weeks does she fly out to forage.

items.label: Beeswax and comb
items.text: Young worker bees produce wax from glands on their abdomen. They shape it into hexagonal cells, a shape that stores the most honey for the least wax.

items.label: Pollination
items.text: While collecting nectar and pollen, bees carry pollen from flower to flower. Many fruit and nut crops, such as almonds and apples, depend heavily on bee pollination.

items.label: Swarming
items.text: When a colony grows crowded, the old queen leaves with about half the workers in a swarm. Scout bees search for a new home and the swarm decides by a kind of vote.

items.label: Winter
items.text: Honeybees do not hibernate. In winter they cluster tightly in the hive and shiver their flight muscles to keep the center warm, living on the honey stored in summer.

items.label: Stings
items.text: Only female bees can sting. A worker's stinger is barbed, so when she stings a mammal it usually stays in the skin and the bee dies.

items.label: The Sun
items.text: The Sun holds more than 99 percent of the solar system's mass. It shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, where the temperature is about 15 million degrees Celsius.

items.label: Mercury and Venus
items.text: Mercury is the smallest planet and closest to the Sun. Venus is the hottest planet, hotter than Mercury, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

items.label: Mars
items.text: Mars is a cold desert planet with the largest volcano known, Olympus Mons. Its red color comes from iron oxide dust, and it has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

items.label: Jupiter
items.text: Jupiter is the largest planet, a gas giant more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Its Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has lasted for centuries.

items.label: Saturn's rings
items.text: Saturn's rings are made of countless pieces of ice and rock, from grains of dust to chunks as big as houses. They are very wide but in most places only tens of meters thick.

items.label: Moons
items.text: Saturn and Jupiter each have well over ninety known moons, and the counts keep rising as surveys find small ones. Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane.

items.label: Ice giants
items.text: Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants because they contain large amounts of water, ammonia and methane. Uranus is tipped on its side, so its poles take turns facing the Sun.

items.label: Asteroid belt
items.text: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. Its largest object, Ceres, is classed as a dwarf planet, and the belt's total mass is less than that of our Moon.

items.label: Pluto
items.text: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. It orbits in the Kuiper Belt, a region of icy bodies beyond Neptune, and has a large moon called Charon.

items.label: Seasons on Earth
items.text: Earth has seasons because its axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees, not because its distance from the Sun changes. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets more direct light and longer days.

items.label: Early bicycles
items.text: The first bicycle-like machine, the running machine of 1817, had no pedals: riders pushed along the ground with their feet. Pedals on the front wheel came decades later.

items.label: Penny-farthing
items.text: The penny-farthing of the 1870s had a huge front wheel because the pedals turned it directly, so a bigger wheel went further per turn. Falls from the high seat were common and dangerous.

items.label: Safety bicycle
items.text: The safety bicycle of the 1880s used a chain to drive the rear wheel, with two wheels of similar size. Its design, with later pneumatic tires, is the basis of most bicycles today.

items.label: Gears
items.text: Bicycle gears change how far the bike travels for each turn of the pedals. Low gears make climbing hills easier; high gears let a rider go faster on flat ground.

items.label: Brakes
items.text: Rim brakes press pads against the wheel rim, while disc brakes grip a rotor at the hub. Disc brakes stop more reliably in wet and muddy conditions.

items.label: Tire pressure
items.text: Correct tire pressure reduces flats and rolling resistance. Road tires often run at 80 to 100 psi, while wider mountain bike tires use much lower pressure for grip.

items.label: Chain care
items.text: A bicycle chain lasts longer when it is cleaned and lightly oiled. A worn, stretched chain wears out the gears, so it is cheaper to replace the chain early.

items.label: Balance
items.text: A moving bicycle stays upright mostly because the rider steers into a fall, moving the wheels back under the body. The front wheel's geometry also helps it steer itself.

items.label: Electric bikes
items.text: An electric bike adds a battery-powered motor that assists the rider's pedaling. Many models stop assisting above about 25 kilometers per hour, depending on local rules.

items.label: Cycling and health
items.text: Regular cycling is low-impact exercise that strengthens the heart and leg muscles. It is easier on the joints than running, which makes it popular for recovery and older riders.
